narrative_purpose: Show why phylogeny trusts inherited construction over outward resemblance: a small double-pulley ankle bone in an early whale fossil ties whales to hippos and other even-toed hoofed mammals despite the adult whale's fishlike body.
subject: An early amphibious whale skeleton with four weight-bearing limbs laid out as a naturalist fossil reconstruction, its hind ankle enlarged in a circular close study to reveal the distinctive grooved double-pulley astragalus; beside it, a hippopotamus hind foot skeleton presents the same grooved ankle-bone shape at matching angle, while a small living whale silhouette swims above as the misleading modern exterior.
scene: An Earth paleontology comparison plate on a dark indigo field, combining fossil slab texture, two precise bone studies, and one restrained living silhouette.
camera: Lateral view of the early whale skeleton and hippo foot, with the two ankle bones oriented identically for direct visual matching.
light: Soft cool museum light across fossil and bone, faint cyan rim on the matching ankle surfaces, living whale silhouette submerged in deep teal haze.
palette: Void indigo ground, warm stone-grey and muted ochre fossil, mist-white bone, ocean teal water silhouette, restrained Pandora cyan on the matching joint surfaces.
style: Painterly paleontological naturalist plate, hand-painted, anatomically precise and quietly dramatic.
detail_level: Crisp on the grooved double-pulley ankle morphology and matching orientation; softer on the whole skeleton and living whale silhouette.
composition: Early whale skeleton spans the lower left, enlarged ankle comparison occupies the centre, hippo foot mirrors it on the right, and the living whale floats small in upper negative space.
consistency_notes: The early whale must be an amphibious four-limbed archaeocete, not a modern whale given fantasy legs. The paired ankle bones should clearly share the same double-pulley construction.
negative_prompt: no text, no labels, no arrows, no chart, no fantasy whale legs, no dinosaur skeleton, no Pandoran species, no photographic museum display, no glossy 3D render, no cartoon or anime style
